idiom_name: final class composition with deinit and weak/unowned back-references
implementation_notes: A reference-type whole owns its class parts under ARC: the whole's deinit runs when the last strong reference to it goes away and releases the parts it holds, so construction and destruction stay symmetric without an explicit dispose call, and destruction is prompt because ARC is not a tracing collector. The Swift book's ARC chapter describes the strong, weak and unowned reference kinds and the strong-reference cycles that must be broken, and its Structures and Classes chapter notes that classes carry identity - which is what a resource-owning part needs. A part that must reach its whole takes a weak reference (the whole may legitimately disappear first) or unowned (the whole provably outlives the part), and the whole must not publish strong references to parts it expects to own exclusively.
pitfalls: Strong reference cycles (a part holding the whole strongly, or two parts holding each other) leak the whole graph: exactly one direction owns and the other is weak or unowned.
unowned crashes at run time when the whole dies first: use it only where the whole's lifetime provably encloses the part's, otherwise weak plus optional handling.
Closures stored in parts capture self strongly by default, so the whole can keep itself alive through its own parts - capture [weak self].

variants.name: Struct parts composed by value (copy semantics, no shared lifecycle)
variants.idiom_name: struct whole with struct parts and mutating methods
variants.implementation_notes: The other Swift realization treats the whole as a value: a struct whose stored properties are its parts, mutated in place through mutating methods or replaced wholesale, with the standard library providing copy-on-write for its collections (arrays share storage until one copy is modified, so the observable behaviour is a copy without paying it eagerly). Copying the whole copies its parts, so there is no aliasing and no ownership problem to enforce - but also no identity: copies evolve independently, parts cannot be shared or observed outside the value that contains them, and a part owning a resource must not be modelled this way. Choose it for pure data aggregations (a layout tree, a parsed document, a computed order) and switch to the ARC variant as soon as a part owns a resource or needs identity.
pitfalls: A struct storing reference-type parts still shares those instances after a copy (the array is copied, the referenced objects are not), so value semantics hold only for value-typed parts.
Value types have no deinit, so a struct cannot own a resource with a lifetime: wrap resources in a class part or close them explicitly.
Mutating a whole with many parts can copy the backing storage unless the copy-on-write optimisation applies; batch edits or keep the parts in a reference type when updates are hot.
